name: Curry leaves
note: In every kitchen, and pushed to the side of nearly every plate. Fry them properly and they get eaten.

name: Drumstick
note: Cheap, in season for months, and mostly used as one piece in a sambar.

name: Ridge gourd (beerakaya)
note: Cooks in under ten minutes. The skin makes a good chutney instead of going in the bin.

name: Bottle gourd (sorakaya)
note: Light and quick. Usually bought only when someone is unwell.

name: Ash gourd
note: Very light, mild, and easy on the stomach late in the day.

name: Methi leaves
note: One bunch flavours a whole dal. Bitter only if overcooked.

name: Raw banana
note: Sits in the kitchen for a week without spoiling. Fries, steams or goes into curry.

name: Banana stem
note: Thrown away by most households. High in fibre and cheap as anything.

name: Amaranth leaves (thotakura)
note: Cooks in five minutes and costs almost nothing.

name: Gongura
note: Sour, strong, and does not need much else on the plate.

name: Cluster beans
note: Slightly bitter, keeps well, and high in fibre.

name: Ivy gourd (dondakaya)
note: Available all year, quick to fry, keeps a week in the fridge.

name: Pumpkin
note: Sweet enough that children eat it without argument.

name: Groundnuts
note: Already in the house for chutney. A handful is a proper snack on its own.

name: Sesame seeds (nuvvulu)
note: Sitting in a jar all year. A spoon dry-roasted goes into anything.

name: Buttermilk (majjiga)
note: Made from what is already there. Better with a meal than any cold drink.

name: Leftover rice soaked overnight
note: The oldest breakfast there is, and it costs nothing.

name: Ragi
note: Usually kept for babies and forgotten after that.

name: Coriander stems
note: Thrown away out of habit. More flavour than the leaves.

name: Guava
note: Cheap, everywhere in season, and more fibre than most fruit that costs three times as much.

name: Papaya
note: Ripens on the counter with no attention. Easy to eat for anyone who chews slowly.

name: Garlic
note: In every kitchen. A few cloves change a plain dal completely.
